Encephalopathy with normal transaminases

A 25-year-old patient treated with valproate becomes lethargic and confused and begins vomiting after topiramate is added. Glucose is normal and liver transaminases are not elevated. Which laboratory measurement is most important for evaluating a recognized drug complication?

  1. Serum troponin
  2. Thyroid receptor antibodies
  3. Urine porphobilinogen as the only test
  4. Plasma ammonia
  5. Serum urate
Answer and explanation

Plasma ammonia

Valproate-associated hyperammonemic encephalopathy can occur despite normal liver tests and is associated with concomitant topiramate.

Option explanations

Plasma ammonia: Valproate-associated hyperammonemic encephalopathy can occur despite normal liver tests and is associated with concomitant topiramate.

Serum urate: Urate does not identify hyperammonemic encephalopathy.

Serum troponin: There is no myocardial injury presentation.

Thyroid receptor antibodies: These do not evaluate this characteristic interaction.

Urine porphobilinogen as the only test: The medication pattern first raises concern for ammonia elevation.
